content: Behçet's disease is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by vasculitis, which can affect multiple organ systems. Mucocutaneous manifestations, including oral ulcers, are common, alongside potential involvement of the central nervous system and skin. This disease can lead to significant complications, such as vision loss, and in severe cases, it can be life-threatening. Oral ulcers are particularly prevalent in Behçet's disease, with an estimated frequency of 97% to 100%. These ulcers can cause substantial discomfort, interfering with essential activities such as eating, drinking, and speaking, thereby significantly reducing the quality of life for affected individuals. Currently, there is no definitive cure for Behçet's disease, and the management of oral ulcers is primarily palliative. The objective of this review was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and safety of various interventions aimed at alleviating pain, reducing the duration and frequency of ulcer episodes, and improving the quality of life in patients with recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS)-type oral ulcers associated with Behçet's disease. To achieve this, comprehensive electronic searches were conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and AMED, up to October 4, 2013. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through the US National Institutes of Health trials register and the World Health Organization Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Authors of studies were contacted when additional information was required. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed pre-specified oral outcome measures, such as pain, episode duration, episode frequency, safety, and quality of life, to evaluate the efficacy of interventions for oral ulcers in Behçet's disease. Trials were not excluded based solely on the outcomes they measured. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were independently performed by two review authors using a standardized data extraction form, following Cochrane's methodological guidelines. A total of 15 trials, involving 888 randomized participants, were included in the review. Of these, 13 trials were placebo-controlled, and three were head-to-head comparisons (two trials included more than two treatment arms). Most of the trials were conducted in Turkey (11 trials), with others in Japan (2 trials), Iran (1 trial), and the UK (1 trial). The majority of the studies used the International Study Group criteria for diagnosing Behçet's disease. Eleven different interventions were evaluated, categorized into topical and systemic treatments. Only one study was assessed as having a low risk of bias. Due to the heterogeneity in trial design, interventions, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis could not be performed. The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, and there was insufficient evidence to definitively support or refute the use of any specific intervention for managing pain, episode duration, or episode frequency associated with oral ulcers, or for assessing the safety of these interventions. The authors concluded that the variability in trial designs, interventions, and outcome measures precluded a meta-analysis. While some interventions showed potential, future trials should adhere to the CONSORT guidelines to ensure methodological rigor. Although the primary focus of many trials on Behçet's disease may not be the reduction of oral ulcers, the reporting of oral ulcer outcomes should be standardized and pre-specified in study methodologies. The development and use of a core outcome set for oral ulcer trials would enhance the consistency and comparability of future research.
